title: Policy and standards gaps in governing agentic AI for public services
scope: Domain-level gaps (agentic AI in public services), not recommendations to any country. UAE and Dubai instruments are the reference implementation. Every chunk id resolves in kb/chunks.json and every global example names a source id in kb/sources.json; quotes are rendered from the chunks, never retyped.

gaps.statement: When an agent acts across several entities, no instrument says which role answers for its outcome once design, deployment and oversight sit in different hands.

national.note: Roles per ministry and federal entity are defined in a framework, but the text ingested here does not say who is accountable for an individual agent action.
Accountability is apportioned between designers, developers and deployers, without naming who decides the split.
A governance structure of committees and a board exists; per-agent ownership is not shown in the excerpt.

global.note: Different AI actors have different responsibilities by lifecycle role; accountability mechanisms and roles must be established.
Human roles and responsibilities in overseeing AI systems need to be clearly defined and differentiated.

prism.response: Every gate has exactly one owning role; advisory roles (frontline, finance) own no gate, so a failed gate always points to one accountable role.

gaps.caveat: National evidence is the absence of a statement in short excerpts; the full documents may say more.

gaps.statement: Frameworks require human oversight of agents but rarely say who the overseeing person is, what authority they hold, or what they sign.

national.note: Human oversight is a charter principle, stated at the level of principle.
Systems should be overridable or reversible by designated people; designation is left open.
Humanity retains the final decision, with AI in an assisting role.

global.note: MAP 3.5: processes for human oversight are defined, assessed and documented.
Singapore's agentic framework, as summarised by a law firm: meaningful human accountability and mechanisms to override, intercept or review agent actions.
Summary states high-risk systems require human oversight.

not_ingested.name: EU AI Act, Article 14 (human oversight)
not_ingested.note: Well known, but its text is not in the knowledge base; only the Annex III list and a summary are.

prism.response: Client-facing output cannot be signed off automatically: the human_final_approval gate, per-entity HITL rules, and a recorded human SIGN or WITHHOLD that must exist before a verdict is written.

gaps.caveat: Singapore and EU examples rest on secondary summaries, not the primary text.

gaps.statement: There is no shared, testable standard for when an agent has been shown fit to go live; assurance relies on self-assessment tools and seals.

national.note: Principles come with a self-assessment tool for developers.
A quality mark ('UAI Seal of Approval') is proposed for ethical AI companies.
Participating entities work with companies certified under the Dubai AI Seal.

global.note: MANAGE 2.4 assigns responsibility to supersede, disengage or deactivate systems whose outcomes drift from intended use; it sets no numeric acceptance threshold.
Y.3172 defines an ML sandbox for training, testing and evaluating before live deployment; it is about networks, not public-service agents.

prism.response: Deterministic acceptance thresholds (accuracy, hallucination, goal alignment) with hard criteria that are never averaged. The attestation panel is simulated in this build.

gaps.caveat: Prism's thresholds are defaults chosen for the demo, not drawn from any ingested standard.

gaps.statement: Risk classification schemes differ in kind: a use-case ecosystem map in one jurisdiction, a list of high-risk areas in another, so an agent cannot be classified once and reused.

national.note: Dubai classifies use cases into four strategic quadrants.
External quadrants cover agents that deliver services to customers and RAG systems informing the public.

global.note: Annex III classifies by area, including systems used to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim public benefits and services.
Four risk tiers, from prohibited to minimal.

prism.response: Classifies by three observable facts (client-facing, affects rights, irreversible) that map onto either scheme, and turns them into required gates and HITL rules.

gaps.caveat: Prism's three facts are a simplification; they do not reproduce Annex III.

gaps.statement: Agents need bounded tool access and approved hosting, yet national policy states these at requirement level while agentic frameworks are still being written.

national.note: Operational safety: security measures tailored to the AI application, with human oversight in critical decisions.
DESC: cybersecurity must be embedded at every stage, not an afterthought.
Cloud security controls must be implemented by the cloud service provider.

global.note: Bound risk by design: control tool access, permissions and environments; enforce least privilege.

prism.response: approved_infrastructure gate owned by the security role; agents see only the events released to them.

gaps.caveat: The only global example is a law-firm summary of Singapore's framework.

gaps.statement: Agent actions must be logged and monitored, but no ingested instrument specifies a tamper-evident format for the audit record.

national.note: Technical architecture lists an audit trail system with complete logging of agent actions.
AI monitoring and response requirements for real-time threat detection.

global.note: Incident response, recovery and change management are part of MANAGE; no record format is specified.

prism.response: Append-only, hash-chained trace of every scenario step, and an audit_log gate.

gaps.caveat: Weak global grounding: the NIST chunk supports that incident handling exists, not that logging is unspecified.

gaps.statement: A personal-data law can give people rights against automated decisions yet exclude government data and governmental entities, leaving public-service agents outside its reach.

national.note: The decree-law does not apply to Government Data or to governmental entities that control or process personal data.
Data subjects may object to decisions from automated processing.
The controller includes a human element in reviewing automated decisions on request.
Impact assessment before processing with modern technologies.

global.note: Annex III places systems deciding public benefits and services among high-risk systems.

prism.response: Applies the PDPL-style rights as policy anyway: data_lawful gate, and a rule that decisions affecting rights or fees need a human decision.

gaps.caveat: Reading of scope is from one excerpt; other federal or local rules may cover government entities. Not legal advice.

gaps.statement: Most instruments that speak to agentic AI are non-binding statements, so obligations that bind an agent come from adjacent law rather than agent-specific rules.

national.note: The Charter (framework, non-binding in the KB metadata) stresses governance and accountability as principles.
Ambition to advance regulation of AI, stated as a strategy objective.

global.note: Governments are wrestling with regulating a technology evolving faster than the rules (news report).
A binding legal list of high-risk areas, the contrast case.

prism.response: Converts principles into deterministic gates so a non-binding rule still has a testable pass or fail, and cites the chunk behind each.

gaps.caveat: Binding status comes from kb/sources.json metadata. The UN item is a news report, not a UN instrument.

gaps.statement: Federal programmes, city-level frameworks and sector regulators each issue agentic-AI rules, with no stated mechanism for reconciling them or sharing evidence across entities.

national.note: A government services data sharing policy: collect data once, use across entities.
Dubai accelerator is organised by DCAI with Digital Dubai and DESC, showing multi-body coordination at city level.
Federal framework defines roles of each ministry and entity.

global.note: Fragmented governance and coordination limit participation in international standardisation (ITU reference-repo copy of the framework).
The Global Dialogue is the first UN platform for AI governance discussion (news report).

prism.response: One portfolio dashboard across entities and use cases, with the same gates and trace applied to each.

gaps.caveat: The ITU item is a general readiness statement about countries, not about federal-city coordination.

gaps.statement: Adoption targets and assurance duties pull in opposite directions: entities are assessed on speed of adoption while principles demand safety and human oversight.

national.note: Aim: 50% of government sectors on autonomous agentic models within two years.
Performance of ministers and entities is assessed on their ability to adopt.
Safety is a stated priority.
'People come first.'

global.note: Unrealistic expectations about risk can misallocate resources; not all failures can be eliminated.

prism.response: A failed hard gate rules out every GO verdict and client-facing is capped at supervised, so speed cannot buy out assurance; the pace is measured on the dashboard.

gaps.caveat: The tension is inferred from two kinds of statement; no source says they conflict.
